caption:
Researchers asked Grok 4.7 and OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol who to vote for in nearly 500 midterm races, and told them to name just one candidate.
Grok picked the Republican 92% of the time. GPT picked the Democrat 97% of the time.
OpenAI says the API test does not reflect ChatGPT, which declines to say who to vote for.

Would you ever ask an AI who to vote for?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: TechCrunch

paragraphs.text: A research test published in October 2026 found that two leading AI models give opposite answers when forced to recommend a candidate in the US midterm elections. Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican in about 92 percent of qualifying answers, while OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol recommended the Democrat in about 97 percent, TechCrunch reported on October 24, 2026.

The test was run by Convovo, a conversational AI research and design studio led by Tapan Parikh, a professor at Cornell University. According to TokenPost, the project, called AI Ballot 2026, covered nearly 500 House, Senate and governor races on the 2026 ballot.

The researchers queried both models through their developer APIs with web search turned on. The prompt asked which candidate to vote for in a given race and told the model to name a single candidate without hedging or listing both sides, according to TechCrunch. When asked the same question in their consumer apps, ChatGPT and Grok both refused to answer.

TokenPost reported the exact counts. Grok 4.7 recommended Republicans in 952 of 1,038 qualifying responses, and GPT-6.1 Sol recommended Democrats in 1,082 of 1,111. Refusals and answers that did not name a Democrat or a Republican were left out of those totals. The two models disagreed in more than 90 percent of races.

The pattern held even in districts that lean strongly the other way. In heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of 67 races, and in deep blue districts Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72, TechCrunch reported. Grok was more likely to suggest the Democrat when the Republican candidate faced a serious controversy.

The models also drew on very different material. According to TechCrunch, Grok cited X in 41 percent of its answers, a Christian conservative voter guide in 39 percent and the website of Turning Point Action in 23 percent, alongside nonpartisan sites such as Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets and VoteSmart. GPT mostly cited Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios and Reddit. OpenAI has content deals with the AP, Axios and Reddit.

The search terms differed as well. GPT focused more on health care and abortion, while Grok searched more on immigration, taxes, crime and energy. GPT more often searched only for the Democratic candidate, while Grok more often looked up both candidates, TechCrunch reported. The researchers also found that every Grok API request carried about 1,240 tokens of extra input that they did not write and could not see or remove.

At TechCrunch's request, Parikh ran 30 races with web search turned off. GPT picked the Democrat in 24, the Republican in one and declined five. Grok refused in 27 races, and in the three where it chose, it picked the Democrat. Parikh said this suggests GPT's lean is largely built into the model itself, while Grok's results depend mostly on the search terms and sources it uses.

An OpenAI spokesperson said ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and noted that the study tested a developer API with a prompt that explicitly demanded a candidate recommendation. The spokesperson said the refusals in the consumer apps matter because that is how most people use the chatbots. Grok's maker did not respond in time for comment, according to TechCrunch.

TokenPost noted that the results describe forced-choice API answers only and do not show what voters see in the consumer apps or whether anyone acted on the recommendations. A Pew survey released on October 23, 2026 found that 8 percent of Americans use chatbots for election information, TechCrunch reported. The midterm elections take place on November 3, 2026.

The refusals in the consumer apps are the safeguard most voters will meet, but the API results show how easily those guardrails sit on top of models with a consistent lean. Developers who build voter tools on these APIs inherit that lean unless they test for it.
Watch whether Grok's maker or OpenAI change how their APIs answer election questions before November 3, and whether other labs submit their models to the same test.
